claim: The wing-hinge contraction contributes to anisotropic tissue flows that reshape the wing blade during pupal stages.
source: At pupal stages, the wing-hinge contraction contributes to anisotropic tissue flows that reshape the wing blade.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct assertion about the biological process being studied.

claim: Wing blade shape change can be quantitatively accounted for on the basis of cell divisions, cell rearrangements and cell shape changes.
source: Here, we quantitatively account for this wing-blade shape change on the basis of cell divisions, cell rearrangements and cell shape changes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cells both generate and respond to epithelial stresses during wing morphogenesis.
source: We show that cells both generate and respond to epithelial stresses during this process, and that the nature of this interplay specifies the pattern of junctional network remodeling that changes wing shape.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including laser ablation experiments and analysis of mutant phenotypes.

claim: Patterned constraints exerted on the tissue by the extracellular matrix are key to force the tissue into the right shape.
source: We show that patterned constraints exerted on the tissue by the extracellular matrix are key to force the tissue into the right shape.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by laser ablation experiments and analysis of dumpy mutants.

claim: A continuum mechanical model quantitatively describes the relationship between epithelial stresses and cell dynamics.
source: We present a continuum mechanical model that quantitatively describes the relationship between epithelial stresses and cell dynamics, and how their interplay reshapes the wing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through the theoretical modeling presented in the Results section.

claim: Laser ablation of the region between the margin of the E-Cadherin:GFP expressing wing epithelium and the cuticle causes the wing epithelium to rapidly retract away from the cuticle within seconds.
source: Although this treatment does not apparently damage either the wing or the cuticle, it causes the wing epithelium to rapidly retract away from the cuticle within seconds (Figure 1A–B′′, Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Laser ablation at any region along the wing blade margin causes epithelial retraction.
source: Laser ablation causes epithelial retraction when performed at any region along the wing blade margin—anteriorly, posteriorly or distally.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental observations of laser ablation at different positions.

claim: The wing is physically restrained by apical extracellular matrix connections to the overlying cuticle.
source: This shows that the wing is physically restrained by apical extracellular matrix connections to the overlying cuticle, and that these connections are required to shape the wing during tissue flows.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the laser ablation experiments showing retraction upon severing the connection.

claim: Apical extracellular matrix connections to the cuticle are required to shape the wing during tissue flows.
source: This shows that the wing is physically restrained by apical extracellular matrix connections to the overlying cuticle, and that these connections are required to shape the wing during tissue flows.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that laser ablation of these connections results in abnormal wing shapes.

claim: Dumpy is a 2.5 MDa protein that is predicted to form filaments at least 1 µm long.
source: Dumpy is a 2.5 MDa protein that is predicted to form filaments at least 1 µm long (Wilkin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to previous work.

claim: Dumpy forms an elastic matrix in the embryonic tracheal lumen.
source: It forms an elastic matrix in the embryonic tracheal lumen, and provides mechanical resilience of tendon cell attachments to the overlying cuticle (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to previous work.

claim: Dumpy provides mechanical resilience of tendon cell attachments to the overlying cuticle.
source: It forms an elastic matrix in the embryonic tracheal lumen, and provides mechanical resilience of tendon cell attachments to the overlying cuticle (Dong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to previous work.

claim: Some dumpy hypomorphs produce wings that are short and misshapen, a defect that arises during pupal development.
source: While dumpy null mutations are lethal, some hypomorphs produce wings that are short and misshapen—a defect that arises during pupal development (Waddington, 1939, 1940).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous work.

claim: The shape of dumpyov1 wings is normal at 16 hr after puparium formation (APF), before molting occurs.
source: The shape of dumpyov1 wings is normal at 16 hr after puparium formation (APF), before molting occurs (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Shortly after molting, when hinge contraction begins, the shape of the dumpyov1 mutant wing blade begins to differ from wild type.
source: Shortly afterwards, when hinge contraction begins, the shape of the dumpyov1 mutant wing blade begins to differ from wild type (WT).
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging comparing wild type and dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: The wing blade epithelium in dumpyov1 mutants retracts abnormally far from the distal cuticle and fails to elongate in the PD axis.
source: The wing blade epithelium retracts abnormally far from the distal cuticle and fails to elongate in the PD axis.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse imaging of dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: Dumpy::YFP is present in the space between the wing margin and the cuticle.
source: (D–E) Show sections in the plane of the wing epithelium near the anterior (D) and posterior (E) margins. Dumpy::YFP is present in the space between the wing margin and the cuticle.
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging of the Dumpy::YFP protein trap shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Dumpy::YFP connects the dorsal wing surface and the cuticle in specific positions.
source: (F–F′′′) Show optical sections orthogonal to the wing epithelium at different proximal-distal positions (indicated in C). Dumpy::YFP connects the dorsal wing surface and the cuticle in specific positions (arrowheads).
evidence: This is directly observed in the imaging shown in Figure 2F-F′′′.

claim: Dumpy::YFP connections between the dorsal wing surface and overlying cuticle lie over the hinge and vein regions.
source: (G) Summarizes the pattern of Dumpy::YFP connections between the dorsal wing surface and overlying cuticle—these lie over the hinge and vein regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed pattern shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Dumpy::YFP connections between the wing margin and cuticle extend around the wing margin except in the posterior/proximal regions.
source: (H) Shows the pattern of Dumpy::YFP connections between the wing margin and cuticle—these extend around the wing margin except in the posterior/proximal regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed pattern shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cutting a dumpyov1 wing between the cuticle and the distal wing blade reveals almost undetectable retraction.
source: Cutting a dumpyov1 wing between the cuticle and the distal wing blade revealed almost undetectable retraction, suggesting that distal attachments of the wing blade to the cuticle are severely compromised.
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments on dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: Distal attachments of the wing blade to the cuticle are severely compromised in dumpyov1 mutants.
source: Cutting a dumpyov1 wing between the cuticle and the distal wing blade revealed almost undetectable retraction, suggesting that distal attachments of the wing blade to the cuticle are severely compromised.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of retraction upon laser ablation in dumpyov1 mutants.

claim: Retraction is still observed when severing is performed between the cuticle and the anterior or posterior margins in dumpyov1 mutants.
source: However retraction was still observed when severing was performed between the cuticle and the anterior or posterior margins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Apical matrix connections to the cuticle are not completely abrogated in dumpyov1 wings.
source: This suggests that apical matrix connections to the cuticle are not completely abrogated in dumpyov1 wings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some retraction still occurs upon laser ablation at anterior and posterior margins.

claim: The orientation of anisotropic stress in dumpyov1 is somewhat splayed and not as well aligned with the PD axis.
source: The orientation of anisotropic stress in dumpyov1 is somewhat splayed and not as well aligned with the PD axis.
evidence: This is observed from circular laser ablation experiments comparing WT and dumpyov1 wings.

claim: Anisotropic tension in dumpyov1 wings tends to be reduced in the central region and increased anteriorly and posteriorly.
source: Furthermore, anisotropic tension in dumpyov1 wings tends to be reduced in the central region and increased anteriorly and posteriorly.
evidence: This is observed from circular laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 2I,I′.

claim: Dumpy-dependent elastic connections are key to the emergence of the stress pattern during morphogenesis.
source: Overall, Dumpy-dependent elastic connections are key to the emergence of the stress pattern during morphogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined observations of dumpy mutant phenotypes and laser ablation experiments.

claim: The area of the wing blade remains fairly constant during pupal morphogenesis, despite the fact that cells are dividing.
source: We showed previously that the area of the wing blade remains fairly constant during pupal morphogenesis, despite the fact that cells are dividing (Aigouy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding with a citation.

claim: Blade area in three analyzed wings is more reproducible than would be expected from the variation in each cellular contribution, if they were independent of each other.
source: Interestingly, blade area in three analyzed wings is more reproducible than would be expected from the variation in each cellular contribution, if they were independent of each other (see shaded regions depicting standard deviations in Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of cellular contributions to area change shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The sum of variances of cellular contributions to area change is about 20 times larger than variance of the sum.
source: To quantify this observation we compared the variance of overall relative area change with the sum of the variances of the cumulative cellular contributions. We find that sum of variances is about 20 times larger than variance of the sum.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data on cellular contributions to area change.

claim: Cellular contributions to area change are not independent and normal variations in the rate of cell division can be compensated by changes in cell area and/or extrusion to maintain wing blade area.
source: This shows that cellular contributions are not independent and that normal variations in the rate of cell division can be compensated by changes in cell area and/or extrusion to maintain wing blade area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is concluded from the statistical analysis of cellular contributions to area change.

claim: Total wing area decreases dramatically when connections at the margin are weakened by dumpyov1 mutation or by laser severing.
source: In contrast to unperturbed WT wings, total wing area decreases dramatically when connections at the margin are weakened by dumpyov1 mutation or by laser severing (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, see dark blue curve).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data comparing WT and perturbed wings.

claim: Connections to the cuticle are required to maintain wing blade area during morphogenesis.
source: Thus, connections to the cuticle are required to maintain wing blade area during morphogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that disrupting these connections leads to decreased wing area.

claim: Wing blade area decrease in dumpyov1 mutant wings is not a consequence of fewer cell divisions.
source: Wing blade area decrease in dumpyov1 mutant wings is not a consequence of fewer cell divisions—cells actually divide more than in WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F,I).
evidence: This is observed from quantification of cell divisions in dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: Cells in dumpyov1 mutant wings have a similar maximum division rate but divide over a longer period of time, resulting in more cells at the end of morphogenesis.
source: Cells in dumpyov1 mutant wings have a similar maximum division rate but divide over a longer period of time, resulting in more cells at the end of morphogenesis (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F, yellow curve).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of cell division rates over time in dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: The reduced wing blade area in dumpyov1 is quantitatively explained by reductions in cell area and by cell extrusions, which more than compensate the increased proliferation.
source: The reduced wing blade area in dumpyov1 is quantitatively explained by reductions in cell area and by cell extrusions, which more than compensate the increased proliferation.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to area change in dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: Reduced epithelial stresses in dumpyov1 wings perturb the balance between cell divisions, area changes and extrusions seen in WT.
source: Thus, reduced epithelial stresses in dumpyov1 wings perturb the balance between cell divisions, area changes and extrusions seen in WT.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing cellular contributions to area change in WT and dumpyov1 wings.

claim: Epithelial stresses are required to balance cell divisions with cell extrusions and cell area changes to maintain area homeostasis during morphogenesis.
source: Taken together, analyzing dumpyov1 and laser-severed wings shows that epithelial stresses are required to balance cell divisions with cell extrusions and cell area changes to maintain area homeostasis during morphogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined analysis of dumpyov1 mutant and laser-severed wings.

claim: Tissue shear in the WT wing blade is oriented in a fan-shaped pattern with a strong PD component.
source: Tissue shear in the WT wing blade is oriented in a fan-shaped pattern with a strong PD component (Figure 5A–A′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved shear patterns shown in Figure 5.

claim: At about 21 hAPF, the shear pattern develops a sharp reorientation between veins L3 and L4, where shear is oriented along the AP axis.
source: At about 21 hAPF, the shear pattern develops a sharp reorientation between veins L3 and L4, where shear is oriented along the AP axis.
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved shear patterns over time.

claim: The region where shear reorients between veins L3 and L4 corresponds to a stripe of Dumpy-containing matrix that attaches the blade to the cuticle.
source: This region corresponds to a stripe of Dumpy-containing matrix that attaches the blade to the cuticle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the shear pattern with the Dumpy distribution pattern.

claim: Shear caused by cell elongation and cell rearrangements (T1 transitions) display significant contributions that are antagonistic.
source: Shear caused by cell elongation and cell rearrangements (T1 transitions) display significant contributions that are antagonistic.
evidence: This is observed from the decomposition of tissue shear into cellular contributions.

claim: T1 transitions cause shear along the AP axis early in the process.
source: Unexpectedly, T1 transitions cause shear along the AP axis early in the process (Figure 5B–B′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved patterns of T1 transition contributions to shear.

claim: Early AP-oriented T1 transitions are opposed by increasing cell elongation along the PD axis.
source: This shear is opposed by increasing cell elongation along the PD axis (Figure 5C–C′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved patterns of cell elongation contributions to shear.

claim: At intermediate and late stages, T1 transitions shift their average orientation to cause PD shear.
source: At intermediate and late stages, T1 transitions shift their average orientation to cause PD shear—at the same time, cells reduce their elongation along the PD axis, causing AP shear.
evidence: This is observed from the time-dependent patterns of cellular contributions to shear.

claim: Cell divisions result in significant shear only during the early stages of wing morphogenesis.
source: The contribution of cell extrusions to tissue shear is negligible (not shown) and cell divisions result in significant shear only during the early stages of wing morphogenesis (Figure 5D–D′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved patterns of cell division contributions to shear.

claim: Correlation effects contribute significantly to tissue shear in the wing.
source: Finally, plotting the contribution D to shear due to correlation effects reveals that these effects do exist in the wing (Figure 5E–E′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved patterns of correlation effects.

claim: During phase I, cells undergo AP-oriented T1 transitions while elongating in the PD axis.
source: During phase I, cells undergo AP-oriented T1 transitions while elongating in the PD axis.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear over time.

claim: Cell divisions during phase I contribute shear along the PD axis.
source: Cell divisions during phase I contribute shear along the PD axis.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear over time.

claim: During phase II, the orientation of T1 transitions shifts to the PD axis and cells relax their shape.
source: During phase II, the orientation of T1 transitions shifts to the PD axis and cells relax their shape.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear over time.

claim: Correlation effects contribute AP shear, and peak roughly at the time that T1's shift their orientation.
source: Correlation effects contribute AP shear, and peak roughly at the time that T1's shift their orientation.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear over time.

claim: The cellular contributions to tissue shear are not independent of each other.
source: The ratio of these values is about 25, indicating that the cellular contributions to tissue shear—like the contributions to area change—are not independent of each other.
evidence: This is calculated from the statistical analysis of cellular contributions to shear.

claim: The overall tissue shear is more reproducible than would be expected from the variations of the cellular contributions.
source: Thus, the overall tissue shear is more reproducible than would be expected from the variations of the cellular contributions.
evidence: This is concluded from the statistical analysis showing that cellular contributions are not independent.

claim: Shear due to correlation effects was mainly generated by correlations between local elongation and rotations.
source: We found that shear due to correlation effects was mainly generated by correlations between local elongation and rotations (Figure 6C–I).
evidence: This is determined from the decomposition of correlation effects shown in Figure 6.

claim: Triangles rotated and sheared in striking spatial patterns that rapidly fluctuate in time.
source: We observed that triangles rotated and sheared in striking spatial patterns that rapidly fluctuate in time (Figure 6C,F,G).
evidence: This is directly observed from the analysis of triangle deformations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Shear and rotation are correlated in regions corresponding to PD-oriented rows that were about 3–7 triangles long.
source: This revealed that shear and rotation are correlated in regions corresponding to PD-oriented rows that were about 3–7 triangles long.
evidence: This is determined from the spatial power spectrum analysis of local tissue rotation.

claim: Correlation effects are mostly accounted for by those cells that are about to undergo a T1 transition within the next 9 frames.
source: Indeed, correlation effects are mostly accounted for by those cells that are about to undergo a T1 transition within the next 9 frames, although they cover only a small fraction of the total area (Figure 6I, Appendix 1, 'Role of T1 transitions in the correlation-induced shear').
evidence: This is determined from the analysis of which cells contribute to correlation effects.

claim: At early times, when T1-induced shear is mainly along the AP axis, connections are typically lost along the PD axis and gained along the AP axis.
source: We observe that at early times, when T1-induced shear is mainly along the AP axis, connections are typically lost along the PD axis and gained along the AP axis (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of connection orientations during T1 transitions shown in Figure 7.

claim: At intermediate times, when the correlation term is maximal, both lost and gained connections were oriented along the PD axis.
source: At intermediate times, when the correlation term is maximal, both lost and gained connections were oriented along the PD axis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of connection orientations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: As T1 transitions begin to cause net PD shear, AP connections are preferentially lost and PD connections are gained.
source: Finally, as T1 transitions begin to cause net PD shear, AP connections are preferentially lost and PD connections are gained (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of connection orientations shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tissue shear is dramatically altered in dumpyov1 mutant wings as compared to WT—instead of shearing in the PD axis, these wings shear on average along the AP axis.
source: Tissue shear is dramatically altered in dumpyov1 mutant wings as compared to WT—instead of shearing in the PD axis, these wings shear on average along the AP axis (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of tissue shear in dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: The rates of AP shear caused by T1 transitions and by correlation effects in dumpyov1 wings are similar to WT and persist for longer times.
source: Examining the different contributions to tissue shear in dumpyov1 wings shows that the rates of AP shear caused by T1 transitions and by correlation effects are similar to WT and persist for longer times.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear in dumpyov1 wings.

claim: AP-oriented T1 transitions and correlation effects are likely to be autonomously driven.
source: Thus, these processes are likely to be autonomously driven.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these processes persist in dumpyov1 mutants where stresses are reduced.

claim: Cell elongation during phase I causes less PD shear in dumpyov1 than in WT.
source: In contrast, cell elongation during phase I causes less PD shear than in WT.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear in dumpyov1 wings.

claim: PD-oriented epithelial stresses must contribute to PD cell elongation.
source: Thus, PD-oriented epithelial stresses must contribute to PD cell elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PD cell elongation is reduced when stresses are reduced in dumpyov1 mutants.

claim: Autonomous cellular processes cause the residual PD cell elongation in dumpyov1 mutant wings.
source: This suggests that autonomous cellular processes cause the residual PD cell elongation in dumpyov1 mutant wings.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some PD cell elongation still occurs in dumpyov1 mutants despite reduced stresses.

claim: PD shear by T1 transitions in phase II is smaller in dumpyov1 than in WT.
source: Finally, PD shear by T1 transitions in phase II is smaller than in WT.
evidence: This is observed from the quantitative analysis of cellular contributions to shear in dumpyov1 wings.

claim: T1 transitions fail to orient as effectively with the PD axis in the dumpyov1 mutant wing.
source: Rather, T1 transitions fail to orient as effectively with the PD axis in the dumpyov1 mutant wing (see shear patterns in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–B′′).
evidence: This is observed from the spatially resolved shear patterns in dumpyov1 mutant wings.

claim: PD cell elongation and PD-oriented T1 transitions clearly depend on tissue stresses.
source: Taken together, the analyses of dumpyov1 wing blades and laser-severed wing blades distinguish autonomously driven cellular processes from those induced by tissue stresses. PD cell elongation and PD-oriented T1 transitions clearly depend on tissue stresses, whereas PD-oriented cell divisions are autonomously driven.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined analysis of dumpyov1 mutant and laser-severed wings.

claim: PD-oriented cell divisions are autonomously driven.
source: PD cell elongation and PD-oriented T1 transitions clearly depend on tissue stresses, whereas PD-oriented cell divisions are autonomously driven.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that cell divisions persist in perturbed conditions where stresses are reduced.

claim: AP-oriented T1 transitions and a corresponding fraction of PD-oriented cell elongation are driven autonomously.
source: AP-oriented T1 transitions and a corresponding fraction of PD-oriented cell elongation are also driven autonomously, as are the cellular events underlying correlation effects.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that these processes persist in perturbed conditions where stresses are reduced.

claim: The cellular events underlying correlation effects are driven autonomously.
source: AP-oriented T1 transitions and a corresponding fraction of PD-oriented cell elongation are also driven autonomously, as are the cellular events underlying correlation effects.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that correlation effects persist in perturbed conditions where stresses are reduced.

claim: The anisotropic part of the shear rate varies linearly with cell elongation.
source: We found that the anisotropic part of the shear rate varied linearly with cell elongation (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is observed from the analysis of circular laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The positive slope of the linear relation between shear rate and cell elongation indicates that the shear modulus K is positive.
source: The positive slope of this linear relation indicates that the shear modulus K is positive.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear fit to the laser ablation data.

claim: In the absence of stress, wing blade cells would spontaneously elongate along the AP axis.
source: This implies that wing blade cells would spontaneously elongate along the AP axis in the absence of stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the positive intercept of the linear fit to the laser ablation data.

claim: In the absence of cell deformation (Q = 0) wing blade cells are exerting higher contractile stress in the PD axis than in the AP axis.
source: Equivalently, in the absence of cell deformation (Q = 0) wing blade cells are exerting higher contractile stress in the PD axis than in the AP axis.
evidence: This is an equivalent interpretation of the positive intercept in the stress-elongation relationship.

claim: Experimental data obtained in WT and dumpyov1 wings fall on similar lines, suggesting that internal mechanical properties of the tissue are not perturbed in dumpyov1 mutant wings.
source: Experimental data obtained in WT and dumpyov1 wings fall on similar lines (Figure 9A), suggesting that internal mechanical properties of the tissue are not perturbed in dumpyov1 mutant wings.
evidence: This is observed from the laser ablation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The continuum mechanical model recapitulates cell shape changes and tissue flow during wing morphogenesis.
source: The continuum mechanical model recapitulates cell shape changes and tissue flow during wing morphogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A single set of parameters accounted well for all time dependent data in unperturbed and mechanically perturbed WT wings.
source: We found that anisotropic stresses in the hinge are small compared to isotropic stresses and therefore we could set ζH and KH to zero. A single set of the remaining 8 parameters accounted well for all time dependent data (see Figure 10B and Figure 10—figure supplement 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fitting procedure and the agreement between model and data.

claim: The continuum theory of epithelia together with appropriate boundary conditions recapitulates the dynamics of cell and tissue shape over 16 hr of morphogenesis.
source: Overall, the continuum theory of epithelia outlined in Equations 1–5 together with appropriate boundary conditions recapitulates the dynamics of cell and tissue shape over 16 hr of morphogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data throughout the time course.

claim: The theoretical approach is a powerful tool for studying how mutations influence specific aspects of cell and tissue mechanics.
source: Thus, this theoretical approach is a powerful tool for studying how mutations influence specific aspects of cell and tissue mechanics.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful application of the model to understand the dumpyov1 mutant phenotype.
